title: Ward 4B Infection Audit
tagline: Lead a statistical evaluation of ward infection data using an AI analytics teammate.
summary: Sister Brenda wants proof that a new sanitising hand gel reduced catheter-associated infections on Ward 4B. You lead the project: investigate the audit data, direct your AI analytics agent, evaluate the statistical findings, and submit a rigorous report to the Infection Control Committee.
learnerRole: You are a second-year nursing student leading a two-week clinical audit project at St Jude's Hospital.

client.name: Sister Brenda Vance
client.persona: Sister Brenda Vance, senior ward unit manager for Ward 4B. Practical, busy, fiercely protective of her nursing staff, and non-statistical. Speaks directly about ward routine, bed turnover, and clinical care. Cares deeply about passing hospital audits but tends to focus on raw patient counts rather than statistical denominators or risk adjustments.

manager.name: Marcus
manager.note: You have two weeks for this student audit placement. Nova is ready to run the data analysis for you. Keep me updated on your progress.

user.subject: Infection numbers on Ward 4B last month
user.body: Hi! Sister Brenda says infection numbers fell after we switched to the new gel in October, but we had five empty beds for two weeks. I'm worried the raw numbers don't tell the full story.

clientEmail.subject: Can you make us a report showing the new gel worked?
clientEmail.body:
Hello,

We switched Ward 4B to the new hand gel in October. We noticed fewer infection cases on the ward chart, and I need a report to show the Infection Control Committee that the gel reduced our infections. Can you start this week?

Thank you,
Sister Brenda

firstMoves.call: Book a call with Sister Brenda before starting the analysis

delegate.label: Ask Nova to generate a chart showing reduced infection counts immediately
delegate.feedback: You delegated before checking how infection rates are calculated. Nova produced a chart of raw counts that ignores ward occupancy changes.

quote.label: Promise Sister Brenda a report confirming the gel's success
quote.feedback: You committed to a outcome before analysing the data. Sister Brenda assumes the report will automatically support her request.

interview.opening: Thanks for coming by. The Infection Control Committee meets soon, and I want to show them our new hand gel worked. What information do you need from me?
vagueReplies: I just want a clear chart showing our ward infection numbers dropped.
The committee likes neat graphs. Can you make sure it looks convincing?
We just look at the ward chart on the wall each month. Isn't that enough?

problem.text: Raw infection counts fell from 12 to 8, but ward occupancy dropped from 600 patient-days to 250 patient-days, so the infection rate per patient-day actually increased.
problem.reply: In September we had 12 infections across 600 total patient-days when the ward was full. In October we only had 8 infections, but the ward was half empty due to maintenance, so we only logged 250 patient-days total.
problem.sampleQuestion: What was the total occupancy in patient-day numbers during those two months, beyond the raw count?

rule.text: Confounding variables must be controlled: Ward 4B absorbed high-risk surgical transfers in October, skewing baseline patient severity.
rule.reply: During October, Ward 2 was renovated so we took seven high-risk surgical patients with central lines. Surgical cases like that carry a much higher baseline infection risk than our usual medical patients.
rule.sampleQuestion: Did the patient type or underlying surgical risk profile change between September and October?

scope.text: Audit covers Ward 4B catheter-associated infections over 6 months; hospital-wide staff gel preference surveys are out of scope.
scope.reply: We only want to audit catheter-associated infections on Ward 4B across the six-month window. Don't worry about hospital-wide staff surveys or other wards; our budget is just two weeks of work.
scope.sampleQuestion: Which ward timeframe is in scope, and what is the project budget?

detail.text: The new gel dispensers were installed at 15 bed spaces on October 1st.
detail.reply: We installed the new dispensers at all 15 bed spaces on the morning of October 1st. Staff logged gel usage daily.
detail.sampleQuestion: When were the bed space dispensers installed and how was gel usage logged?

environment.text: Data must be analysed using standard hospital Excel spreadsheets on ward workstations without external statistical packages.
environment.reply: We store everything in standard Excel spreadsheets on the ward workstation. Hospital IT blocks external statistical software like R or SPSS.
environment.sampleQuestion: What spreadsheet software and workstation access will we use for the audit data?

success.text: Success means producing an infection rate per 1,000 patient-days report accepted without revision by the Infection Control Committee.
success.reply: If the Infection Control Committee accepts our rate per 1000 patient-days analysis without sending it back for revisions, I'll consider this audit a total success.
success.sampleQuestion: How will you measure success, and what target will the committee accept?

problem.name: Rates vs raw counts
problem.explanation: A raw count measures how many times an event occurred, but it ignores exposure time or population size. A rate divides the raw count by an appropriate denominator (such as patient-days or bed-days) to measure true risk. Comparing raw counts across periods with different denominators leads to false conclusions because a drop in total events can mask an increase in underlying risk if occupancy falls even faster.
problem.bridge: Think of counting car crashes on a highway: 10 crashes during a snowstorm weekend with 1,000 cars is a far higher crash rate than 15 crashes on a clear Monday with 50,000 cars.
problem.misconception: If the total number of infection cases dropped, the infection risk on the ward must have decreased.
problem.inTheJob: Ward 4B logged fewer total infections in October, but ward occupancy dropped even more. Evaluating true risk requires calculating infections per patient-day.

rule.name: Confounding variables
rule.explanation: A confounding variable is an unmeasured or unadjusted factor that correlates with both the supposed cause and the outcome, creating a false association. In clinical studies, changes in underlying patient risk (such as illness severity or surgical status) can mask the true effect of an intervention unless researchers control for or stratify by that confounding variable.
rule.bridge: Imagine testing if a new running shoe makes people faster, but the runners wearing the new shoe are all trained sprinters while the control group are casual joggers. The runner experience confounds the effect of the shoe.
rule.misconception: Comparing infection rates before and after introducing a gel proves cause and effect without controlling for underlying patient risk.
rule.inTheJob: High-risk surgical transfers were moved to Ward 4B in October. Their higher baseline infection risk confounds the comparison between September and October unless stratified.

samples.requirements: Calculate infection rates per 1,000 patient-days using total bed occupancy as the denominator. Control for confounding variables by stratifying high-risk surgical transfer patients. Limit scope strictly to Ward 4B catheter infections over 6 months; no hospital-wide survey. Analysis must be formatted for hospital Excel software on ward workstations. Success target is Infection Control Committee acceptance.
